chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Umar ibn Yazid, from Abu al-Ala', from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

Umar ibn al-Khattab was brought a woman who had attached herself to a man from the Ansar, and she loved him but could not find a way to do so. She went, took an egg, removed the yolk, and poured the white onto her clothes and between her thighs. Then she came to Umar and said, 'O Commander of the Faithful, this man took me in such-and-such a place and disgraced me.' Umar was about to punish the Ansari, so the Ansari began to swear, while the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) was sitting and saying, 'O Commander of the Faithful, be firm in my case.' When the young man had sworn much, Umar said to the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him), 'O Abu al-Hasan, what do you see?' The Commander of the Faithful looked at the white on the woman's garment and between her thighs, suspecting that she had contrived it for that purpose. He said, 'Bring me hot water that has been boiled with a strong boil.' They did so. When the water was brought, he ordered them to pour it on the spot of the white. The white cooked/stiffened. The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) took it and put it in his mouth. When he recognized its taste, he spat it out. Then he turned to the woman until she confessed to that, and God, might and glory be to Him, saved the Ansari from Umar's punishment.

key_terms.اَلْأَنْصَارِ: The Ansar (Helpers), the tribe of Medina

ai.seo_question: How did Imam al-Sadiq help Umar ibn al-Khattab distinguish between a real and fake accusation of seduction?
ai.summary: This well-known judicial precedent (hukm) highlights Imam al-Sadiq’s (peace be upon him) keen observational skills and his role as a wise advisor to the Umayyad caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab. By identifying the coagulation of egg white in hot water, the Imam exposed the woman’s clever stratagem to fabricate evidence of seduction, thereby ensuring justice for the Ansari man. This incident is frequently cited in Shia jurisprudence to illustrate the importance of contextual evidence and the caliph’s reliance on the Ahl al-Bayt for legal discernment.
